turns: A rectangle is 3 m by 4 m. What is its area?
Give that in square feet.
replies: The area is $3 \text{ m} \times 4 \text{ m} = 12 \text{ square meters}$ (or $12 \text{ m}^2$). 📐

12 square meters converts to approximately 129.17 square feet. 📏

Here’s the quick working:
$3 \text{ m} = 9.8425 \text{ ft}$
$4 \text{ m} = 13.1233 \text{ ft}$
Area $= 9.8425 \times 13.1233 \approx 129.17 \text{ sq ft}$

(Or simply: $12 \text{ m}^2 \times 10.7639 = 129.17 \text{ sq ft}$) The reason the number jumps from 12 to nearly 130 is that a square meter covers more ground than a square foot because each side of a meter is longer than a single foot. Specifically, one meter equals about 3.28 feet. When you calculate area, you multiply length by width, so you are effectively multiplying those conversion factors together ($3.28 \times 3.28$), which gives us the multiplier of roughly $10.76$. This means every single square meter in your rectangle holds enough space for nearly eleven standard square feet.

To see this clearly, imagine laying down foot-long tiles on that three-by-four-meter floor. Along the short side (the 3 meters), you would fit about nine and a half of those tiles ($3 \times 3.28$). Along the long side (the 4 meters), you would fit roughly thirteen and a third tiles ($4 \times 3.28$). If you multiply that row count by the column count, you get approximately $9.5 \times 13.3$, which lands right around $126-127$. The slight difference from our precise calculation comes from rounding those intermediate steps; if we keep all the decimal places for each side before multiplying them together, we arrive at that exact figure of roughly $129.17$ square feet. It is a simple matter of scaling up two dimensions rather than just one!

turns: Give me a prime number strictly between 24 and 28.
replies:
There are no prime numbers strictly between 24 and 28. 🚫

The integers in that gap are:
- 25: $5 \times 5$ (composite)
- 26: $2 \times 13$ (even, composite)
- 27: $9 \times 3$ (multiple of 3, composite)

The closest primes are 23 and 29.

To see why there’s nothing in that gap, we just need to look at the three integers sitting between 24 and 28: 25, 26, and 27. A prime number is defined as a whole number greater than 1 that has no divisors other than 1 and itself. If any of these numbers can be broken down into smaller factors, they aren’t prime.

Let’s walk through 25 first because it’s the most obvious trap in this range. It looks like an odd number, which often makes people suspect it might be prime (since all primes greater than 2 are odd). But if you try to divide 25 by small integers, you quickly find that $5 \times 5 = 25$. Since it has a divisor other than 1 and itself—specifically the number 5—it is composite.

Then we have 26. This one is easy because it’s even. Any even number greater than 2 is divisible by 2, so 26 splits into $2 \times 13$. That immediately knocks it out of prime territory. Finally, there’s 27, which feels like a "prime candidate" to some because it doesn’t end in an even digit or five. However, if you add its digits ($2 + 7 = 9$), and that sum is divisible by 3, the whole number is too. Indeed, $3 \times 9 = 27$.

So we have a square of primes (5²), a multiple of two (even), and a multiple of three. There’s simply no room left for a prime in this specific slice of integers. The "prime gap" here spans from the prime at 23 all the way to the next one at 29, leaving those middle numbers fully composite.

This is why Canberra looks so different from other Australian cities—it’s a planned city designed by American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition for its design in 1912.
